deep.reconstruction:
Overview. This is a scrap or doodle sheet. Its substantive content is a set of tables of quadratic residue characters. Around them are short scratch computations, ornamental shaded grids, pen trials and unrelated words. The words look like place and person names: Romagna, Peter I, Rasumovsky, Blaubeuern, and probably 'Brunsvic' (Braunschweig). The previous page is dated 11 Oct 1795 and holds long decimal periods of 1/p and 1/p^2 (1/529 = 1/23^2, 1/361, 1/343, 1/289, 1/243). This sheet therefore almost certainly belongs to Gauss's Brunswick or early Göttingen period of 1795. That is when he was collecting residue tables by induction, just before his first proof of quadratic reciprocity (8 April 1796).

(1) Top dot table. The columns are headed -1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 23. The rows are the odd primes p = 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 23. A dot in cell (p, q) evidently marks the character of q modulo p. In modern terms, the dots mark the q with Legendre symbol (q/p) = +1 (my reading). The computed residue sets are:
- p=3: {7, 13, 19}
- p=5: {-1, 11, 19}
- p=7: {2, 11, 23}
- p=11: {3, 5, 23}
- p=13: {-1, 3, 17, 23}
- p=17: {-1, 2, 13, 19}
- p=19: {5, 7, 11, 17, 23}
- p=23: {2, 3, 13}

Several features of the image match this reading:
- Rows 13 and 17 carry a dot in the -1 column, since -1 is a residue of primes ≡ 1 mod 4. Rows 3, 7, 11, 19 and 23 do not.
- Row 19 is the densest row, with five residues.
- Row 23 has few dots.

The heavy horizontal line between rows 13 and 17, and a vertical rule in the middle, partition the table. They may simply be visual aids. Dot positions cannot be resolved with full certainty from the image, so 'dots = residues' (rather than non-residues) is my interpretation.

(2) Second table. It has the same row labels. The column header, written inverted, is +1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 23. The same information is displayed as solid cross-hatched blocks. The very first column (+1) is shaded for every row, since 1 is always a residue. This supports reading shading = residue. The other shaded grids are partly ornamental elaborations of the same black/white residue pattern: the hatched 'quilt' grids, the black-and-white checker with lines, and the bottom-left X-shaped checker next to columns of circled dots.

The point of such a two-way table (prime p against prime q) is to compare (q/p) with (p/q) by reflecting across the diagonal. This is exactly the empirical route to the reciprocity law:
- If p ≡ 1 or q ≡ 1 mod 4, the symbols agree.
- If both p and q are ≡ 3 mod 4, they are opposite.
- The supplements are (-1/p) = (-1)^((p-1)/2) and (2/p) = (-1)^((p^2-1)/8).
The -1 and 2 columns encode precisely these supplements.

(3) Scratch arithmetic. Only the pieces I can verify:
- 133 appears repeatedly, and 17689 = 133^2 is written under a small stacked computation (176 / 397 / 22 / 180...).
- 30976 = 176^2 is written beside '3976' and '318'.
- 1724 and 431 appear together, and 1724 = 4·431.
- 1761 and 12 also appear. Other numbers may be dates (1724, 1761), consistent with the historical names on the page.
- The upper-right blocks are not reconstructable from the image: 3325, 557, 556 221, 224, a bracketed division-like scheme 50377 / 50020 / 267025 / 566755 / 75, and a small digit table 3 5 6 6 6 / 0 0 0 0 / ...
- The pairs '26 24 / 26 24 / 9 8 / 9 8' are not interpretable with confidence.

The small grid with dots in cells (3 dots and 2 dots), and the clusters of dots and circles, look like counting or trial doodles.
errors: No mathematical error can be established. The reconstructed residue table is internally consistent with the Legendre symbols where the dots are legible.
Several scratch numbers (397, 22, 180, 3976, 318, 215589, 50377 etc.) cannot be tied to a verifiable computation. Any apparent arithmetic among them is uncheckable from the image.

results.what: Two-way table of quadratic residue characters (q/p) for q in {-1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 23} and odd primes p ≤ 23, drawn as dots and as shaded blocks
results.modern_name: Table of Legendre symbols / quadratic residue table (empirical basis of quadratic reciprocity and its supplements)
results.usually_credited_to: Empirical reciprocity: Euler (1740s–1783) and Legendre (1785). First proof: Gauss (1796, Disquisitiones Arithmeticae 1801). Gauss is known to have found the law by induction from such tables in 1795.

deep.surprise_reason: The page is an early (c. 1795) worksheet of quadratic residue tables of the kind Gauss tells us he used to discover reciprocity by induction. It is consistent with the known story and Disquisitiones art. 99ff. It is a nice archival witness but contains nothing new, and the rest is doodles and trivial arithmetic.

checkable.asserts: The 2 and -1 columns obey the supplementary laws

transcription_corrections: The second grid header is written inverted and reads '+1 2 3 5 7 11 13 17 19 23' with rows 3…23. It is a shaded version of the same residue table.
'Eroufrie [?]' is most likely 'Brunsvic' (Braunschweig), written in a decorative hand.
'17689' = 133^2 and '30976' = 176^2; the associated stacked figures are partial multiplication work, not independent numbers.
'B L' and 'RamR' are pen trials or ornamental letters, not mathematics.
